issues.title: Nakis: a TLS tunnel proxy built around connection reuse and write coalescing (efficiency first, circumvention effect unverified)
issues.body:
Hello all,

I would like to share a small project and ask for feedback from people who know this area better than I do. Nakis is a SOCKS5-in, TLS-tunnel-out proxy written in Go. Its main goal is transfer efficiency: get a ready tunnel to the application with as little waiting as possible, and keep per-write overhead low. Resistance to DPI was a secondary concern. I have not tested it against any real censor, so please read the DPI-related parts as hypotheses.

Repo: https://github.com/n-yarvex/nakis (MIT). The wire format and notes on the reference implementation are in doc/SPEC.md.

## Where the waiting goes

Most browser sessions are short, so the cost is dominated by setting up a tunnel: TCP, TLS, then whatever authentication the protocol adds. Nakis tries to take that off the critical path.

**Pre-connected pool.** The client keeps tunnels that have already finished the TLS handshake and authentication. A new session takes one from the pool and starts sending right away. This is always on, because turning it off could only make things slower.

**Reuse.** When a session ends, each side sends a zero-length frame (called NAP in the spec) for its own direction. Once both have been seen, no error occurred, and the tunnel has not used up its lifespan, it goes back to the pool and the next session reuses it without a new handshake. Each tunnel draws its own lifespan: a number of sessions (by default between 4 and 8) and a byte budget (log-uniform between 8 and 256 MiB), so there is no fixed "Nth session" or "Nth byte" boundary.

**Racing when the pool is empty.** The client dials several candidate addresses: the first two immediately, the rest staggered by 50 ms. The first to finish the handshake serves the session. The others are not thrown away; they go into the pool. The idea is mostly for lossy links and servers with several addresses, where one slow path should not stall everything.

## Write coalescing

Many proxies write each application read as its own frame. Nakis puts a queue (a "Box") in front of the tunnel and decides when to flush ("Gate"). One frame is one Write, which under TLS ends up in one record.

- If the queue is empty and the last data arrived at least 40 µs ago, the chunk is sent immediately. This is meant to keep interactive small writes from being delayed.
- Otherwise chunks queue up and are packed greedily into one frame, up to `send_pack`. A chunk is never split; what does not fit waits for the next frame.
- The queue is flushed when it reaches `send_pack`, or comes within `send_tail` bytes (default 512) of it.
- If it is not full, a 250 µs timer runs. If more data arrived in the meantime, it waits another tick, up to `send_quiet` x 4 ticks. With `send_quiet=4` that means at most about 4 ms of merging while data keeps arriving, and at most 250 µs once it stops.
- Large reads (32766 bytes or more) bypass the queue after flushing what is already queued, to keep ordering.
- The server has a second layer: small upstream frames are merged into writes of up to `merge_pack` (default 20 KiB) towards the target. When the queue reaches `max_queue`, the server stops reading the tunnel and TCP backpressure slows the client.

The trade-off is plain: under sustained small writes, latency can rise by up to `send_quiet` milliseconds in exchange for fewer, larger records.

## Shaping the first packets

The first few packets of a session (up to eight per direction) get a randomly drawn target size, per tunnel, per session, per direction. The target is reached by coalescing application data first. Padding (a frame with length 0xFFFF) is only used if the data has not filled the target after 2 ms, so this does not work like a conventional padding scheme. For the first packet only, that wait is an added latency of up to 2 ms. Observatory: return independent snapshots under the status lock
issues.body:
`Observer.GetObservation` returns the internal status slice and its protobuf objects while background probes update and prune them. Callers can therefore observe changes after the method returns, race with updates during serialization, or accidentally mutate observer state.

Clone the observation under the existing status mutex. The returned message owns its slice, status objects, and nested messages; serialization happens after the lock is released. Probe scheduling, balancing behavior, and the protobuf API are unchanged.

Tests cover preservation of fields, snapshot stability after updates/additions/pruning, caller mutation of the slice and nested HealthPing message, empty results, and concurrent updates/pruning/readers/serialization. The isolation regression fails on unmodified main.

Validation:
- Windows: Observatory package tests, 100 repetitions of the new snapshot tests, balancer regression tests, and `go vet ./app/observatory/...` passed.
- Linux: `go test -race ./app/observatory/... -count=10` and balancer regression tests with `-race` passed in a separate validation branch containing the same source commit.
- Linux: `go vet ./app/observatory/...` and the repository-wide `vformat` check passed. The local Windows format check reported CRLF checkout differences; the clean Linux checkout passed.
- Full router tests were attempted locally but require the absent `resources/geosite.dat`; the targeted balancer tests passed.

Validation run: https://github.com/wywywywycloud/Xray-core/actions/runs/43646303751

Refs #5117. This fixes snapshot safety in the existing Observatory API; it does not implement the remaining outbound-management features.

issues.title: UDP: avoid info-level read failure after local session termination
issues.body:
When the UDP idle timer or owner closes a session while `handleInput` is reading, termination cancels the context and interrupts the pipe. The read can return `io.ErrClosedPipe` after the loop's context check, producing an info-level `failed to handle UDP input` message for a local close.

Downgrade that error to debug only when this connection's local termination flag is set. Make the existing flag atomic because termination, input handling, and dispatcher reuse inspect it across goroutines. Unrelated read errors, closed-pipe errors without local termination, and parent cancellation alone retain the existing logging behavior. EOF handling and cleanup order are unchanged.

Tests exercise the real pipe interruption path, idle timeout, concurrent/repeated close, wrapped errors, unrelated errors during shutdown, parent cancellation, EOF, and the close callback count. The regression test fails on unmodified main with the original info-level message.

Validation on Windows/amd64:
- `go test ./transport/internet/udp -count=1` passed.
- `go test ./transport/internet/udp -run TestHandleInputTermination -count=100` passed.
- `go vet ./transport/internet/udp` and `git diff --check` passed.
- Local race-detector execution was unavailable: the environment has no CGO C compiler. Linux runtime tests were not run locally.

Refs #4621. This addresses local UDP termination only; it does not suppress remote resets or change general connection-error handling.

issues.title: conf: support process-scoped fingerprint weights in TLS
issues.body:
Adds `tlsSettings.fingerprintWeights`, resolving an explicit weighted browser policy once per process into the existing protobuf `Fingerprint` field. New TCP connections, HTTP clients, and reconnects reuse the selected profile. Equivalent policies share the process-wide result from the common resolver.

**Depends on #7406; merge #7406 first.** This branch is based directly on the resolver branch and does **not** depend on REALITY PR #7407. Until #7406 is merged, GitHub's main-branch diff also includes that dependency. Review TLS-only changes in [this comparison](https://github.com/wywywywycloud/Xray-core/compare/codex/weighted-fingerprint-resolver...codex/tls-weighted-fingerprints). Related: #7405 (selection lifetime revised to once per process).

Example fragment inside `tlsSettings`:

```json
"fingerprintWeights": {
  "firefox": 9,
  "chrome": 70,
  "edge": 12,
  "safari": 9
}
```

Weights are relative probabilities per process, not proportions of connections. The field conflicts with a nonempty `fingerprint`; invalid policies fail before selection. Resolution occurs after TLS configuration checks succeed, with debug logging of the selected name. Existing single-fingerprint/default/random behavior and protobuf definitions remain unchanged. TLS transport call sites consume the resolved name through their existing paths; no handshake or ALPN rewriting behavior is changed. XDRIVE's ALPN warning now examines the built TLS configuration, including the selected profile.

Supported paths include RAW, gRPC, WebSocket, HTTPUpgrade, XHTTP/XDRIVE over TCP, MASQUE H2, and FinalMask XDNS HTTPS over TCP. Configuration checks reject paths that cannot apply uTLS profiles: mKCP, Hysteria, XHTTP/XDRIVE H3, MASQUE's QUIC path (including its default), XDNS H3 or non-HTTPS resolvers, and Realm's Go TLS client. The checks match each transport's actual ALPN switch rather than rejecting every list containing h3.

Browser dialer is rejected for weighted WebSocket/XHTTP configurations when configured or active at build time. Embedders can enable it later through Reload; since it then owns the handshake, the browser path emits a once-per-process warning that Xray fingerprint settings do not apply. This warning also covers legacy fingerprint settings; it does not block or reconfigure browser connections. No runtime policy metadata is added to protobuf.

Unlike modern REALITY's additional hybrid-key-share requirement, ordinary TLS supports all four example aliases in the local integration tests, including Edge. This does not guarantee acceptance by any particular remote server or DPI. Aliases retain their existing uTLS-version semantics.

Validation (Go 1.27.4, Windows amd64):

- `go test ./infra/conf -run "TestTLSFingerprintWeights|TestXDriveHTTP1ALPNWarning" -count=1 -timeout 90s`
- `go test ./infra/conf ./transport/internet/tls ./transport/internet/browser_dialer ./transport/internet/websocket ./transport/internet/splithttp ./transport/internet/xdrive ./transport/internet/finalmask/xdns -count=1 -timeout 120s`
- `git diff --check`

New tests cover normalized-policy stability, equivalence to a selected legacy configuration, invalid inputs/conflicts, unchanged legacy modes, no selection on invalid TLS configuration, transport propagation and rejection, browser configuration, nested XDNS, Realm rejection, and XDRIVE warnings with/without ECH. A local certificate-pinned TLS/HTTP integration test verifies each of Chrome, Firefox, Edge and Safari across two fresh connections. All listed tests passed. The race detector was not run locally (no C compiler installed).

issues.title: conf: support process-scoped fingerprint weights in REALITY
issues.body:
Adds client-side `realitySettings.fingerprintWeights`. Configuration building validates all candidates, resolves the policy once per process using the shared resolver, and stores the selected name in the existing protobuf `Fingerprint` field. Reconnecting does not reselect; RAW, XHTTP and gRPC use their existing REALITY client path.

**Depends on #7406; merge #7406 first.** This branch is stacked on its resolver commit. Until that dependency is merged, the GitHub diff against main also includes PR 1. The REALITY-only changes can be reviewed in [this comparison](https://github.com/wywywywycloud/Xray-core/compare/codex/weighted-fingerprint-resolver...codex/reality-weighted-fingerprints). Related feature request: #7405 (revised to process-lifetime selection).

Example fragment inside client `realitySettings`:

```json
"fingerprintWeights": {
  "firefox": 15,
  "chrome": 70,
  "safari": 15
}
```

Weights are relative selection probabilities per process, not connection shares. Equivalent policies reuse the same process-wide result. The new field conflicts with a nonempty `fingerprint` and is rejected in server configurations. Selection happens only after the remaining client configuration checks succeed. Debug logging identifies the selected name. Existing single-fingerprint/default/random behavior, protobuf definitions, and connection code are unchanged.

All candidates are checked locally before selection (including cache hits): ClientHello construction must succeed, offer TLS 1.3 with a 32-byte session ID, and provide a suitable X25519 key. The current pinned REALITY server additionally requires an X25519MLKEM768 share before standalone X25519; the new weighted mode validates that requirement as well. No network connections are made during validation.

**Compatibility finding:** the currently pinned uTLS `edge` alias is Edge 85 and lacks the required hybrid share. Consequently the earlier illustrative Firefox 9 / Chrome 70 / Edge 12 / Safari 9 policy is rejected, with a candidate-specific error, instead of producing intermittent failures. Old explicit fingerprints remain accepted under their existing rules; this stricter validation is scoped to the new weighted mode and current REALITY-server compatibility. Browser aliases can change when uTLS is updated.

Validation (Go 1.27.4, Windows amd64):

- `go test ./infra/conf -run TestREALITYFingerprintWeights -count=1 -timeout 90s`
- `go test ./infra/conf ./transport/internet/reality ./transport/internet/tls -count=1 -timeout 120s`
- `git diff --check`

Tests cover equivalent-policy stability, equivalence to the selected legacy configuration, conflicts/invalid candidates/server rejection, legacy modes, no selection on invalid client configuration, validation of previously cached policies, propagation through RAW/XHTTP/gRPC stream configs, and real local REALITY client/server handshakes with authenticated bidirectional application data for Chrome/Firefox/Safari. The local target's post-handshake camouflage cache is seeded to avoid external probes. The race detector was not run locally (no C compiler installed).

issues.title: conf: add process-scoped weighted fingerprint resolver
issues.body:
Adds a shared configuration-layer resolver for explicit, weighted browser fingerprint policies. Each normalized policy selects once per process and reuses that result across subsequent resolutions. This is groundwork for TLS and REALITY configuration support; it does not expose a new JSON setting in those configurations yet.

Related to #7405. This implements the revised selection lifetime: **once per process per distinct policy**, rather than once per connection as originally described in the issue.

Equivalent policies share a cached result regardless of key order, name casing, or proportional scaling of weights. Distinct policies select independently. Positive uint64 weights are checked for overflow; unknown names, duplicate normalized names, and special random/randomized/Go TLS/unsafe modes are rejected. Browser aliases and explicit registered browser versions are accepted. Aliases retain their existing uTLS version semantics.

Validation is separate from selection. Selection uses crypto/rand without modulo bias, serializes concurrent initialization, and does not cache entropy failures or fall back to a default profile. The process-lifetime cache intentionally retains each resolved policy until process exit. Existing GetFingerprint and the startup-selected random preset are unchanged.

Future TLS/REALITY integrations can validate their transport-specific constraints, resolve the policy, and write the selected name into the existing protobuf Fingerprint field. Those integrations, transport compatibility checks, user-facing documentation, and protobuf policy support are outside this PR.

Validation (Go 1.27.4, Windows amd64):

- `go test ./infra/conf -run TestFingerprintWeights -count=1`
- `go test ./infra/conf ./transport/internet/tls`
- `git diff --check`

Tests exhaust the example's weighted intervals and cover invalid input, JSON numeric types, equivalent policies, concurrent resolution, independent policies, a fresh resolver lifetime, entropy failure/retry, single-candidate selection, and preservation of the legacy random preset. The race detector was not run locally (no C compiler installed).

Tunnel inbound: Close idle fake UDP sockets in TPROXY mode
issues.body:
Fixes #5263 (closed as not planned).

### Problem

With `tproxy` on a Tunnel (dokodemo-door) inbound, replies go through `PacketWriter`. It opens a fake UDP socket bound to each remote address that sends a reply ([dokodemo.go:231-245](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/proxy/dokodemo/dokodemo.go#L231-L245)). The sockets are closed only in `Close()` ([:266-273](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/proxy/dokodemo/dokodemo.go#L266-L273)), when the UDP session ends ([:189](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/proxy/dokodemo/dokodemo.go#L189)).

A cone session ends after its client port has been silent for 2 minutes ([worker.go:397](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go#L397)). Only client packets count as activity ([worker.go:200](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go#L200)). A P2P application sends from one port to many peers and is never silent for 2 minutes. Its session keeps one fake socket for every peer that ever replied.

On a router with transparent proxy (TPROXY → dokodemo-door) xray grew by about 1450 sockets and 7 MB of RSS per hour: 6524 open fds 4.5 hours after a restart that followed an OOM kill. #5263 shows the same growth.

### Reproduction

`05-xray-fakeudp-repro.sh` (below) runs as a normal user in network namespaces: `unshare -Urn sh 05-xray-fakeudp-repro.sh ./xray 10 300`. The client sends from one UDP port to 10 new peers per second. Every 10th datagram goes to a peer first contacted more than 180 s ago. Peers echo from the address they were sent to. Inbound:

```json
{"listen": "0.0.0.0", "port": 1100, "protocol": "tunnel",
 "settings": {"allowedNetwork": "udp", "followRedirect": true},
 "streamSettings": {"sockopt": {"tproxy": "tproxy"}}}
```

```sh
iptables -t mangle -A PREROUTING -i <client-if> -p udp -j TPROXY --on-port 1100 --tproxy-mark 1
ip rule add fwmark 1 lookup 100
ip route add local 0.0.0.0/0 dev lo table 100
```

### Results

`main` at c456141, linux/amd64, 10 new peers/s, open fds of the xray process:

| time, s | main | with this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 60 | 609 | 609 |
| 120 | 1209 | 1209 |
| 180 | 1809 | 1508 |
| 240 | 2349 | 1501 |
| 300 | 2888 | 1495 |

Both builds: 3000/3000 replies, 120/120 replies from old peers, none from a wrong address.

Router, arm64, v26.7.28 with the same change: 6524 fds and growing before; about 880 without a trend 15 hours later, 575 five days later.

### Change

- `PacketWriter` records when each remote last sent a reply.
- `WriteMultiBuffer`, at most every 30 s, closes and forgets the fake sockets of remotes silent for 2 minutes. The next reply from such a remote opens a new socket through the existing path.
- The socket of the original destination (`w.conn`) is never closed early. Datagrams without a `UDP` address are written to it too ([:255](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/proxy/dokodemo/dokodemo.go#L255)). Before, one write error on it closed it for the rest of the session.
- On a write error the map entry is deleted instead of set to `nil`.

The sweep runs on the writer goroutine: no new goroutine, no lock. 2 minutes matches the session timeout in `worker.go`. If replies stop completely, the sweep waits for the next write, which is the old behavior.

### Tests

- `TestSweepIdleClosesOnlyIdleFakeSockets` in `proxy/dokodemo/fakeudp_sweep_test.go`.
- `go build ./...`, `go test ./proxy/dokodemo/...` (also `-race`), `go vet ./proxy/dokodemo/`, `go run ./infra/vformat/main.go -mode check` pass with go1.27.0.

issues.title: Observatory: fix data race in observation results
issues.body:
## Summary

Fix a data race in ordinary Observatory's `GetObservation` by returning an independent snapshot of the observation results.

## Problem

`GetObservation` currently returns a new `ObservationResult` containing references to the observer's internal status slice and messages.

Background probes update these statuses under `statusLock`, while consumers may read or serialize them after `GetObservation` returns.

This can cause concurrent reads and writes in routing strategies, metrics, and gRPC protobuf serialization.

The issue was reproduced on the current upstream `main` with Go's race detector, including a protobuf serialization error:

```text
WARNING: DATA RACE
size mismatch: calculated=22, measured=31
```

## Solution

Deep-clone the observation result while holding the existing `statusLock`:

```go
o.statusLock.Lock()
defer o.statusLock.Unlock()

return proto.Clone(&ObservationResult{Status: o.status}), nil
```

This ensures that callers receive an independent snapshot, including nested protobuf messages and unknown fields.

The existing synchronization mechanism, protobuf API, health checks, and routing behavior remain unchanged.

## Testing

Added two regression tests:

- **Snapshot isolation:** verifies that returned results do not share mutable state with the observer or other snapshots, including nested messages and unknown fields.
- **Concurrent access:** exercises status updates, additions, removals, and concurrent reads with protobuf serialization.

Both tests reproduce the original issue. The snapshot test also fails when using a mutex without deep copying.

Validation completed successfully:

- `go test -race ./app/observatory/...`
- `go test ./app/observatory/... ./app/router/... ./app/metrics/...`
- Xray build
- Formatting and diff checks

## Performance

Deep cloning introduces O(n) copying under the existing mutex. Benchmarks covering 2, 20, and 200 outbound statuses confirm the expected linear cost.

The fix intentionally favors correctness and minimal changes over additional synchronization complexity.

issues.title: Routing: add server-only VMess UUID routes and online user cache
issues.body:
Allow ordinary VMess clients to select declared server-side routes by changing UUID bytes 7 and 8, with only the server upgraded and no account flag required. `userRoute` is the shared routing matcher; `vlessRoute` keeps its existing behavior.

README.md is unchanged in the PR diff.

## Behavior and compatibility

- Generate aliases only for explicit `routing.rules[].userRoute` values applicable to the inbound and user, including existing exact/regexp user matching. Destination-dependent conditions remain routing conditions; Lua-only routing declares no aliases.
- Preserve exact configured UUIDs and the original account's email, policy, statistics and API identity. The experimental account flag and wire extension have been removed completely. Account JSON/protobuf definitions and client encoding match the pre-feature source; no account option or wire field is added.
- Admit connections after normal authenticated header checks. Registration IDs, route generations and pending-change checks reject stale candidates across account/rule changes, including removal and re-addition of the same account object. Closed validators cannot rebuild catalogs.
- Retain identity history during an inbound's lifetime so a removed exact credential cannot become another user's generated alias. Different original route bytes mark the 14-byte identity ambiguous and disable its aliases. Exact credentials remain usable. History is not persisted: independently revocable users and credential rotations must use distinct non-route UUID bytes.
- Align Unicode email removal with the inbound's lowercase index. Retain AuthID replay entries for the full inclusive timestamp-validity interval using 241-second buckets; accepted clock skew and wire encoding remain unchanged. This retains more replay records under sustained traffic.

## Cache and resource bounds

Only authenticated online/recent accounts populate the prepared cache; there are no IP/source-address hints. Idempotent connection leases expire two minutes after the final close. Route changes preserve live leases and idle deadlines without refreshing recency. Search and eviction share one recency list, immutable provider declarations are copied before filtering, and rejected cache growth does not evict unrelated entries.

Per inbound: 64 MiB prepared-key payload, a 128 MiB raw-alias-key limit, and two concurrent alias scans. Oversized live catalogs preserve exact credentials while rejecting aliases. Metadata, replay records and temporary old/new catalog overlap are additional memory. Occupied scan slots can reject further alias handshakes, including hot-cache users; exact credentials bypass those slots.

The amd64 AES-NI/SSE4.1 search accelerator retains all ten AES rounds in a 68-byte schedule and rechecks candidates with the standard-library decoder. Unsupported CPUs, `purego`, and Go FIPS mode select the standard-library fallback. This is not a cryptographic certification or a claim of VLESS-equivalent lookup cost.

## Validation

- VMess, router/command, routing features and configuration tests passed, along with the complete VMess `purego` tests and repository formatting.
- After removing the experimental account flag, all 160 published-binary compatibility cases passed again using clients 1.8.24, 25.12.8 and 26.11.9: 120 ordinary VMess/VLESS cases in both directions, 33 UUID-only/negative/legacy-route cases, and seven byte-identical old-config compilation cases. Coverage includes TCP/UDP, AES-GCM/ChaCha20-Poly1305, Mux, and route values 0/300/65535.
- Known-answer AES plus 4,096 differential decryptions; malformed headers and replay; identity collisions/revocation; concurrent account/rule changes; and 4,000-operation cache lifecycle checks passed. Selected regressions also passed 30 repetitions at each of 1/2/4 CPUs with shuffled order, Go pointer checking, and runtime CPU-feature fallback.
- Windows executable and Linux amd64/arm64 VMess cross-builds passed. The full network scenario package passed

issues.title: HTTPUpgrade client: Close the connection when the upgrade fails
issues.body:
When the upgrade request could not be sent, or the server did not answer with a valid "101 Switching Protocols", the dial returned the error and left the TCP connection open until the garbage collector closed it.

With "fingerprint": "unsafe", a failed TLS handshake is one of these cases. Go's TLS does the handshake at the first write, and here the first write is the upgrade request.

issues.title: DNS outbound: End UDP sessions once their queries are answered
issues.body:
A UDP session of the DNS outbound never reads EOF, so it lasts until the inbound drops it or its idle timer fires. The timer looks for activity once per connIdle, so a session answered right away ends after two periods, ten minutes by default. The dokodemo-door inbound drops idle UDP after two to three minutes; the TUN inbound never does. Stub resolvers and dnsmasq usually send each query from a new source port, so every query holds a session with three goroutines that long.

On my test bench (linux/arm64, FakeDNS, 5000 queries at 50 per second, a new port per query) RSS grew from 40 MB to 187 MB through dokodemo-door and to 180 MB through TUN, where the goroutines were gone only ten minutes after the last query.

I track the queries a UDP session still owes an answer, hijacked or sent upstream, by ID and question, so a repeated answer settles nothing. While any is open the session keeps connIdle, so a slow lookup is not cut; one second after the last answer it ends, which still leaves room for AAAA sent after A from the same socket. TCP, the session of Xray's own DNS client, a session with more than 256 open queries and a connIdle below one second work as before.

issues.title: XHTTP server: Drop resent packet-up uploads instead of reading them again
issues.body:
## Why

A packet-up upload can reach the server twice. A CDN or a reverse proxy may send a POST to the origin again after a timeout, and a client may resend a packet that got a 502 or 504 although it went through. The server already drops a copy of a seq it has fully read. It does not handle a copy that is in the queue while the first one is only partly read. `uploadQueue` pushes the unread rest of a packet back into the heap with the same seq, so the next `Read` may pop the full second copy and return it from the start. The stream is then silently corrupted, and nothing in the logs says why.

With this change a duplicate of any seq is dropped, whatever sent it. It also makes it safe for a client to resend failed uploads, which is #7371.

## What changed

- The unread rest of a packet is kept in `uploadQueue.partial` instead of going back to the heap, and `nextSeq` moves on as soon as the packet starts being read.
- Any other copy of that seq is then below `nextSeq` and is dropped by the existing check.

## Testing and limits

- New `Test_UploadQueueDropsDuplicateSeq` pushes seq 1 twice before seq 0 and reads with an 8 KiB buffer. On main it fails with a corrupted stream, with this change it passes.
- `go test ./transport/internet/splithttp/... ./infra/conf/...` passes, also with `-race`.
- Nothing changes for clients that do not resend.
- A copy that arrives before its seq is read still takes a place in the reorder heap and counts towards `scMaxBufferedPosts`.

issues.title: XHTTP client: Add `scMaxPostRetries` to resend failed packet-up uploads
issues.body:
## Why

packet-up is there for CDNs and proxies that don't pass a streaming upload, so every packet goes through them as its own POST. Today the first POST that fails closes the whole connection, with everything that runs inside it. Behind a CDN a single 502 or 504 is not rare even when the server is fine, the CDN may time out waiting for the origin or lose its connection to it. An ordinary HTTP client would just send such a request again. Here it is safe to, since every packet carries its seq and with #7370 the server drops duplicates. It can't be done higher up, VLESS and mux don't see the packets.

One example we measured. With Yandex Cloud CDN about 2% of requests got a 504 after the CDN waited 5 seconds for the origin, and some got a 502. 3 of 10 uploads up to 3 MB broke with the current client and all 10 went through with resending. On a CDN emulator that checks integrity it was 12 of 12 against 4 of 12.

## What changed

- New client option `scMaxPostRetries`, 0 by default. Above 0, a packet that is not answered with 200 is sent again up to `scMaxPostRetries` times before the connection is closed as it is today.
- A 504 from a CDN comes only after several seconds. So one more copy is sent when the last copy was fully written but got no answer in 2 seconds. The first 200 wins and the other copies are cancelled. A packet with no 200 in 30 seconds fails the connection.
- The server gives up once it holds more than `scMaxBufferedPosts` packets after a missing seq. So with resending on, seq N is sent only after seq N minus `scMaxBufferedPosts`/2 is answered.
- `PostPacket` now uses the context it is given. The normal path detaches it from the connection as before, and the resend path uses it to cancel copies that are no longer needed. A cancelled copy no longer marks the HTTP/2 client as closed, otherwise each resend would open a new connection.
- With `scMaxPostRetries` at 0 the upload loop works as before.

## Why it is off by default

A resent packet may reach the server twice, for example when the CDN delivered it and then timed out waiting for the answer. A server without #7370 may read that copy again and corrupt the stream, and the client cannot tell which server it talks to. So resending stays off unless the server is known to drop duplicates. It could become the default some releases later.

## Testing and limits

- New `Test_PacketUpRetriesFailedPost` puts an HTTP/2 proxy in front of the server that answers 502 to the first upload of seq 1. The echo goes through with `scMaxPostRetries` 2 and times out with 0.
- `go test ./transport/internet/splithttp/... ./infra/conf/...` passes, also with `-race`.
- Together with #7370 I also ran a proxy that forwards every third upload to the server and still answers 504, so duplicates do reach the server. The stream stays intact.
- Only packet-up. A stream-up or stream-one upload is one long request, and the client cannot know how much of it the server got.
- It does not help when the CDN fails the download GET.
- HTTP/1.1 `PostPacket` does not read the answer status, so there only failed writes are resent. The browser dialer has no write callback, so it only resends on errors.
- The extra copy after 2 seconds assumes the server answers soon after the body is written. On a slow uplink with large `scMaxEachPostBytes` the body may still sit in the socket buffer, and a copy is sent for nothing. Behind a CDN small posts are the norm, so this should be rare. 2 and 30 seconds are constants.

issues.title: Happy Eyeballs: add successDefinition to race until TLS handshake completes
issues.body:
## Motivation

When the server's domain resolves to several IPs, Happy Eyeballs is supposed to pick a working one. In Russia, however, some ISPs (the DPI boxes installed at them) drop the ServerHello for some of these IPs while TCP to them still connects. Which IPs are affected differs from one ISP and region to another and changes over time: an IP that is blocked for one client works for another, so removing it from DNS would only break it for everyone else. Happy Eyeballs today ends the race at the first TCP connection, so it happily picks such an IP, and then the TLS or REALITY handshake can never complete. A retry usually picks the same IP again, because it wins the TCP race again. In this situation the current Happy Eyeballs is of no use at all, even though other IPs of the same domain work fine.

## What this PR adds

A new optional field `successDefinition` in `sockopt.happyEyeballs`:

| Value | The race is won by |
|---|---|
| `tcpConnected` (default) | the first established TCP connection, as before |
| `tlsHandshakeComplete` | the first connection that completes the TLS or REALITY handshake |

```json
"sockopt": {
  "domainStrategy": "UseIP",
  "happyEyeballs": {
    "tryDelayMs": 250,
    "maxConcurrentTry": 4,
    "successDefinition": "tlsHandshakeComplete"
  }
}
```

Without `successDefinition`, or with `tcpConnected`, nothing changes. Without TLS or REALITY, `tlsHandshakeComplete` is the same as `tcpConnected`.

The behaviour follows section 6.1 of Happy Eyeballs v3, which says clients SHOULD wait for the TLS handshake to complete before canceling other attempts: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-happy-happyeyeballs-v3/
Chromium's Happy Eyeballs v3 implementation does the same: a TCP-based attempt runs the TLS handshake inside it and completes only when the handshake does, and an attempt counts as slow (so the next one starts) if TCP and TLS together take longer than the connection attempt delay:
- https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/net/socket/tls_stream_attempt.cc
- https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/net/http/http_stream_pool_attempt.cc

Happy Eyeballs v3 is still a draft, and browsers do not use it by default yet: in Chromium it is behind the `HappyEyeballsV3` feature, which is disabled by default, and Firefox enables it only in Nightly.

## How it works

- The scheduler of `TcpRaceDial` is reused as is (`tryDelayMs`, `maxConcurrentTry`, `prioritizeIPv6`, `interleave`); only the attempt it runs differs. With `tcpConnected` the attempt is the same system dial as before.
- With `tlsHandshakeComplete` every attempt goes through TCP dial to one IP → FinalMask (if any) → the transport's own TLS or REALITY handshake. Only the TCP destination changes from attempt to attempt; masks apply to each attempt separately, exactly as on a normal dial.
- An attempt keeps its `maxConcurrentTry` slot until its handshake ends, and a hanging handshake does not stop the scheduler from starting the next attempt after `tryDelayMs`.
- Losing attempts are stopped by closing their connections. Transports that leave the handshake to the first write (gRPC, and HTTPUpgrade and XHTTP with Go TLS) get it completed inside the race, so a connection is never handshaked twice.
- The race happens under the same conditions as the TCP race in `DialSystem`: `domainStrategy` set, at least two IPs, no `dialerProxy`, non-zero `tryDelayMs` and `maxConcurrentTry`. Otherwise the transport dials exactly as before.

All covered transports now dial through `internet.DialTCPWithHandshake(ctx, dest, streamSettings, handshake)`. `handshake` is a function that wraps the TCP connection with the transport's TLS or REALITY client; it holds the same code the transport used to run right after its own TCP dial.

Transports covered: RAW (TLS, REALITY), WebSocket, HTTPUpgrade, gRPC (TLS, REALITY), XHTTP over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 (TLS, REALITY), MASQUE over HTTP/2. For XHTTP the race runs once per new physical connection. UDP

issues.title: Feature request: configurable TLS fingerprint selection with weights and an explicit allowlist
issues.body:
As one of many VPN services using Xray, we’d find it useful to configure multiple TLS fingerprints, assign each a percentage (chance of choosing specific fingerprint on connection, analogous to `random`), and explicitly exclude fingerprints that do not work in our target networks. The core would select a fingerprint once per new connection according to those weights.

For example: **Firefox 9%, Chrome 70%, Edge 12%, Safari 9%**, with `ios`, `android`, and `chrome-133` excluded.

In our experience, Russian DPI blocks connections using those three fingerprints in some cases. Unrestricted random selection is therefore risky: individual connections may fail simply because an incompatible fingerprint was selected.

We previously used Firefox because it worked well in our environment. However, what works today may change, and having 100% of connections share the same normalized TLS fingerprint could itself help TSPU identify VPN traffic.

Weighted selection would reduce this uniformity, while explicit control over the allowed fingerprints would help preserve reliability. This would not make VPN traffic indistinguishable from browsers, but it would give operators a practical way to manage that tradeoff.

issues.body:
### Problem

`OriginalDst` in `transport/internet/sockopt_darwin.go` reports success when the `DIOCNATLOOK` ioctl fails:

```go
if _, _, errno := syscall.Syscall(syscall.SYS_IOCTL, fd, DIOCNATLOOK, uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&nl))); errno != 0 {
	return net.IP{}, -1, os.NewSyscallError("ioctl", err)
}
```

`err` is the `os.Open("/dev/pf")` result from the top of the function, which already returned early if it was non-nil, so `err` is always `nil` here — and `os.NewSyscallError` returns `nil` for a nil error. The `errno` the ioctl returned is dropped.

Both callers (`tcp.GetOriginalDestination`, `udp.RetrieveOriginalDest`) only test `err != nil`, so they build a destination from the zero IP and port `-1`: `net.IPAddress(net.IP{})` returns a nil `Address`, `net.Port(-1)` wraps to 65535, and `IsValid()` does not catch it since it only checks `Network != Network_Unknown`.

### Fix

Report `errno`. It is already the branch condition, so the error is always non-nil.

### Notes

Two further issues in this function, left alone because Darwin's `struct pfioc_natlook` cannot be verified (no `net/pfvar.h` in the SDK) and the path has no test coverage: `nl.proto` is always `IPPROTO_TCP` although `hub_darwin.go` reaches this function for UDP, and `nl.af` is never set to `AF_INET6` although the result is switched on `nl.af`. `sockopt_freebsd.go` sets both.

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go run ./infra/vformat -mode check` and `go test ./...` are clean on this branch; the three geodata-dependent packages fail identically on unmodified `main` here because `geoip.dat` / `geosite.dat` are absent locally.

tun: end UDP flows and cancel dispatches when the inbound closes
issues.body:
## Problem

Closing a core instance that has a `tun` inbound leaves its UDP flows alive, and everything they hold with them.

- `Handler.Init` detaches the handler's context from the instance (`core.ToBackgroundDetachedContext`), and nothing cancels it on `Close`.
- `stack.Close` resets the TCP connections and closes the sockets opened by `DialUDP`, but never touches the UDP flow table (`udpConnectionHandler.udpConns`).

So each UDP flow's reader keeps waiting on its packet queue after `Close`, which pins its XUDP mux session, the mux `ClientWorker` and that worker's connection to the server.

Measured in a client that embeds the tun inbound and restarts the instance per session (goroutine origins from `runtime.Stack`): about 80 goroutines, 0.8 MB of live heap and stacks, and one established outbound connection leaked per instance, with no decay over 8+ minutes. After 25 instances: 1600 goroutines, all created by `tun.(*udpConnectionHandler).HandlePacket`, `mux.(*ClientWorker).Dispatch`, `mux.NewClientWorker` and `mux.(*DialingWorkerFactory).Create`, and 17 established connections to the server.

## Fix

- `Handler` owns a `cancel` for its detached context and calls it in `Close` before closing the stack, so in-flight dispatches unwind (also the ones not blocked on the reader).
- `stack.Close` ends every UDP flow (`udpConnectionHandler.closeAll`): their readers get EOF, the dispatches return and release their outbounds. The flow table also refuses new flows from then on, mirroring `handleTCP`'s `closed` check: a packet already in flight between the stack closing and the tun closing used to open a fresh flow (and, with a mux outbound, dial a worker) during shutdown.

The remaining XUDP mux workers then close on the mux client's idle check (two 16 s monitor ticks after their last session), after which goroutines and heap are back at the baseline and no server connections remain.

## Verification

- New tests: `TestUDPHandlerCloseAllEndsFlows` (flows end on close, a late packet opens none) and `TestHandlerCloseCancelsDispatches` (a dispatch that is not reading returns when the handler closes). `go test -race ./proxy/tun/` passes.
- With the patch, 20 instance start/stop cycles end with 0 established connections to the server and the baseline goroutine count; without it, 17 connections and 1600 goroutines that never go away.

With Xray's TUN as the system VPN, an app that reads a response until the server closes waits about 1 s more than it should on every such connection. The outbound already knows the response is over, but TUN keeps the app's connection open until the whole dispatch ends, and that happens only after `uplinkOnly`. Examples are HTTP/1.0 without `Content-Length`, RTSP (Moonlight in #5845) and simple request and reply protocols. With this change the app gets the end of the response right away

- TUN sends FIN to the app as soon as the outbound is done with the response. The app can still send, and the connection is closed as before when the dispatch is over
- the lightweight TCP stack gets `CloseWrite` for that
- the rest of the core still closes links in pairs, as agreed in the thread

issues.title: TUN inbound: Route each new UDP destination, keeping FullCone NAT within a route
issues.body:
The UDP FullCone table (#5509) is keyed by the source only, and only the first packet of a session is routed, so later destinations of that source reuse its outbound. As the TUN never sees a socket close, a port that the OS reuses before the session expires inherits the old route. For example, DNS on a port last used by a direct or blocked flow never reaches the DNS outbound, and a resolver that retries from the same port (mDNSResponder) keeps the stale session alive.

Now a new destination is routed once, with fake IPs judged by their domain and no DNS lookup made. It then joins its source's session for the same rule, or gets a session of its own. Destinations of one rule still share a session, so FullCone is kept within a rule, and a balancer picking another outbound doesn't split it. Routing runs off the goroutine that reads the tun. WireGuard and MASQUE servers are unchanged.

Checked on a real utun on macOS with the system resolver: DNS on a reused port is answered and destinations of one rule leave from one port, while on main the DNS goes nowhere and every destination leaves from the first one. A new destination costs about 2 µs more; established flows and throughput are unchanged.

AI disclosure: this PR was completed using Claude Opus 5.5.

issues.title: XHTTP server: unblock writes and serialize connection close
issues.body:
## Summary

An XHTTP response write can hold the connection mutex while blocked on a slow reader. Closing the logical connection then waits on that mutex, including when a proxy inactivity timeout cancels the business context while the HTTP request stays open.

Signal closure before waiting for the writer and interrupt an active write using `http.ResponseController`. Serialize the complete transition with `sync.Once` so concurrent business/handler closes join the deadline call and the writer before `ServeHTTP` returns.

```text
Close (once)
  signal closure
  interrupt active write
  wait for writer completion
```

## Evidence

- Added `TestConcurrentCloseWaitsForDeadline`, using a real HTTP test server and a gated response writer. The gates ensure the business close owns the first deadline call before the handler closes.
- Upstream implementation: fails with `Close waited for the blocked writer without interrupting it`.
- An unserialized close transition: fails with `deadline call outlived ServeHTTP during concurrent Close`.
- Commit `8628110`, rebuilt with Go 1.27.3 on Linux/amd64: `go test -buildvcs=false ./transport/internet/splithttp -count=1` passes (`ok`, 2.434s).
- Bounded loopback `packet-up` fixtures run against a binary rebuilt from commit `8628110`: peer half-close and an internal inactivity timeout with the HTTP request still open both finish with `CLOSE_FRAMES=0`, `WRITE_FRAMES=0`, and `CLOSE_WAIT_CONNECTIONS=0`.

## Merge Danger

**Door:** Two-way.

**Blast Radius:** XHTTP shutdown. Active I/O is interrupted on close; the existing transport tests cover normal completion.

issues.title: XHTTP: Add configurable error responses
issues.body:
## What

Adds an optional `errorResponse` object to the XHTTP inbound settings, replacing the bare status-only rejections with a service-consistent appearance.

Currently every rejected request is answered with a bare status code: no body, no `Content-Type` (Go's default "404 page not found" or nothing at all). From the terminating side (CDN, reverse proxy, monitoring) a server that answers *every* unknown path with a naked status code and no content type does not look like a normal service.

- `body` and `contentType` apply to every error response the hub writes (404 unknown path, 400/405/409/413/500 etc.), giving all rejections a uniform, service-consistent appearance.
- `statusCode` overrides the status for requests failing the padding validation — the effective authentication gate — allowing 403 semantics instead of the default 400.
- When `errorResponse` is unset, the behavior is unchanged.

Example:

```json
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/api/v2/stream",
  "errorResponse": {
    "statusCode": 403,
    "body": "{\"error\":\"forbidden\"}",
    "contentType": "application/json"
  }
}
```

Resulting surface: unknown paths → `404 {"error":"forbidden"}`, the API gate without valid padding → `403` with the same body — a coherent API host instead of a bare 404/400 machine.

## Notes

- Server-side only. Round-trips through `extra` like the other settings.
- `config.pb.go` regenerated with protoc v6.33.5 / protoc-gen-go v1.36.11 (matches all existing `.pb.go` headers; unmodified proto regenerates byte-identical with this toolchain).
- Proto field `errorResponse = 31` — merges cleanly alongside #7247 (`responseHeaders = 30`); both features are independent.

## Tests

- `Test_WriteErrorResponse`: bare default when unset, configured body + content type, padding-reject status default (400) and override (403).
- `go test ./...` passes locally across all packages, except the pre-existing network-dependent `TestQUICNameServer` in `app/dns`, which fails identically on pristine `main` in my environment (no QUIC egress).

issues.title: XHTTP: Add configurable response headers
issues.body:
## What

Adds an optional `responseHeaders` map (`map<string, string>`) to the XHTTP inbound settings, giving the server control over the headers it writes on responses.

Currently the hub hardcodes a set of response headers: the CORS block for the browser dialer (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`), `X-Accel-Buffering`, `Cache-Control` and the SSE `Content-Type`. With `responseHeaders` an operator can add, override, or remove any of them, as well as set arbitrary extra response headers.

## Semantics

- A key that doesn't collide with a default header is added to every response.
- A key that matches a hardcoded header overrides it.
- An empty value removes that header from the response entirely (including the hardcoded ones).
- When `responseHeaders` is unset, the behavior is byte-identical to before.

Example:

```json
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/api/v2/stream",
  "responseHeaders": {
    "Server": "nginx",
    "Cache-Control": "no-cache, no-transform",
    "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "https://example.com",
    "X-Accel-Buffering": ""
  }
}
```

## Why

- The CORS headers only matter for the browser dialer; a plain server deployment currently emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on every response, which is undesirable behind a specific origin and gets flagged by security reviews.
- Reverse-proxy and CDN setups sometimes require specific response headers (`Server`, `Via`, custom headers) or different cache semantics.
- Operators running behind intermediaries may want the response header set to stay consistent with the profile of the service they front, instead of carrying markers that no other service on that endpoint emits.

## Notes

- Server-side only; the client ignores it. It round-trips through `extra` like the other settings.
- `config.pb.go` regenerated with protoc v6.33.5 / protoc-gen-go v1.36.11 — the header matches all existing `.pb.go` files (`check-proto` passes; I verified the unmodified proto regenerates byte-identical with this toolchain first).

## Tests

- `Test_SetResponseHeader`: default / override / removal via empty value.
- `Test_WriteResponseHeader_ResponseHeaders`: CORS default, override, removal, custom header addition, origin echo.
- `go test ./...` passes locally across all packages, except the pre-existing network-dependent `TestQUICNameServer` in `app/dns`, which fails identically on pristine `main` in my environment (no QUIC egress).

issues.title: grpc: close cached clients with their outbound handler
issues.body:
Related to #7177. Requesting review of resource ownership, shutdown semantics, and API compatibility

## Problem

Outbound gRPC clients are cached by destination and MemoryStreamConfig, but core shutdown never closes or removes them. In an embedding process that stays alive, clients can retain connections and continue reconnecting after their core has stopped.

## Change

Give memory stream settings synchronous close-hook registration, and close the resources from their owning outbound handler. Register each ClientConn for exact-entry cache removal and ClientConn.Close. Refuse both reuse and creation after owner closure starts; racing creation must either register for cleanup or close its unpublished client. Cleanup runs outside the settings/cache locks, and concurrent Close callers wait for the same result.

The supported Instance lifecycle is single-start. Each fresh core retains separate ownership even when endpoint and outbound tags match. No per-run generation model, idle-timeout change or per-RPC closure of the shared ClientConn is added.

## Validation

- Synthetic regression reproduces the problem on v26.3.27 and main da2248c.
- `go test -race ./transport/internet ./transport/internet/grpc -count=1 -timeout=120s` passes on this exact branch.
- Official `go run ./infra/vformat/main.go -mode check -pwd ./` passes.
- Tests cover two live cores, sibling streams, normal/MultiMode, fresh-core cycles, failed-start cleanup, multiple destinations, owner/acquisition races, cancellation/backoff and forced dialerProxy lookup contention with Manager.Close.
- Earlier candidate testing also ran the target race suites five times and the dialerProxy test ten times. Those results are supplementary, not a claim that the whole upstream suite passes.

## Review questions / limits

- Handler.Close previously always returned nil. This candidate propagates cleanup errors. Is propagation preferred, or should transport cleanup be logged while preserving the existing return policy? Embedders must distinguish a cleanup error from a still-running core.
- MemoryStreamConfig with resource/mutex state must not be copied; direct external transport callers must close their settings.
- Manager.RemoveHandler still bypasses Handler.Close. XHTTP/nested download settings and TUN eventfd cleanup remain unfixed.
- No general multi-instance guarantee for Xray's other process-global networking state, TLS/Reality/masking matrix, or physical Android packet boundary is claimed.

This is intended as a draft for ownership/API review, not a claim that the Android product defect is resolved.

issues.title: Finalmask: Add the `lua` mask (noise's `script` moves there)
issues.body:
#7174 bolted a second Lua mask onto header-custom, which was the wrong way around. One `lua` mask covers all of it now: it is both a `tcpMasks` and a `udpMasks` entry, and the script decides what it does by the hooks it defines.

-- `HandleHeader(stream, address, role)`, TCP: a free handshake before any traffic, with `stream:Write`, `stream:Read` and `stream:Sleep`. Return a string or an error and the connection is dropped
-- `HandleHeaderWrite(header, address, role)` and `HandleHeaderRead(packet, address, role)`, UDP: prefix every packet with a header, and strip it on the other side by returning its length, or `nil` to drop the packet
-- `HandleNoise(plan, address, role)` is the old noise hook, so `noise`'s `script` is gone (it has not been in a release yet)
-- `role` is `client` or `server`, so one file serves both ends
-- a hook the script does not define is not wrapped at all: a noise only script leaves TCP connections alone and never touches a packet
-- the module is `xray.finalmask` now, with `Random` and `RandomBetween`

```json
{
    "udpMasks": [{"type": "lua", "settings": {"script": "mask.lua", "reset": "30-60"}}]
}
```

Per call it takes at most 64 noise packets and 65535 bytes of noise, 1024 bytes of header, and 65535 bytes each way in a handshake. A packet hook gets 1s, a handshake 30s. A UDP header is one Lua call per packet, the benchmarks in the package cover its cost.

The static lists can follow later, the same script can already do what they do.

XHTTP: packet-down in stream-down with downlink keep-alive
issues.body:
# XHTTP: packet-down in stream-down with downlink keep-alive

Follows RPRX's packet-down design in https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/6755#issuecomment-5720463978, which was written while closing the earlier downlink-resume attempt (#6755). That attempt was rejected because "restore connection" is too complex, with latency, ACK and so on. This one does not attempt connection restoration at all. No reconnection, no state machine, nothing to tune: each stream-down GET stays a single request; if the GET dies, the connection dies the ordinary way.

## Problem (from #4846)

CDNs kill a stream-down GET on body inactivity. This matters during uploads: with packet-up the uplink posts keep flowing, but the downlink proxy payload only arrives while the origin sends, so during a pure upload the GET idles and gets cut. Same story for any target that goes quiet for a while after responding.

## What this PR adds

When enabled on both ends, the stream-down response body is cut into packet-down frames with the five elements from the design comment:

- omittable session id excerpt: first 8 bytes of the session id, present on data and keep-alive frames (absent in stream-one where the session id is empty)
- omittable packet seq: uint64, counting data/keep-alive frames per stream-down GET
- mandatory type: data or padding
- mandatory length: uint16
- payload

Use today is the first one from the design comment: downlink keep-alive. While the downlink has been idle for a whole period, the server writes a padding frame (base62, in the spirit of tokenish x-padding) instead of staying silent. Everything the dispatcher sends rides in data frames, which is what lets the client tell padding apart from payload safely; the seq keeps the format ready for the future uses listed in the design comment (retransmission, multi-path-down) without another wire change.

h1, h2 and h3 are covered, since the framers sit on the body, not on a specific transport. stream-one gets the same treatment on its single response body. Browser dialer is out of scope for now: it has no place to read the response header that confirms the framing.

## Negotiation

Strictly opt-in and per request, so old servers are unaffected and nothing breaks behind middleboxes:

1. client config has packetDown: XHTTP stream requests not used as pure uplink (stream-down GET, stream-one request) carry X-Packet-Down: 1
2. server has packetDown configured and sees the marker: it answers with X-Packet-Down: 1 on the response, and frames; without the confirmed header the client never parses frames
3. any other combination: byte-identical wire format as today

## Config

```jsonc
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/sh",
  "packetDown": {              // absent = disabled, as today
    "keepAlive": true,
    "keepAlivePeriod": "10-30",  // seconds; padded when inactive this long. defaults to 10-30
    "keepAliveLength": "24-64"   // padding size. defaults to 24-64
  }
}
```

Server side is the same block in the inbound; the server only honors the feature when the client asks.

## Not in this PR (deliberately)

- obfs of the frames (later, per the design comment)
- retransmission, multi-path-down, same-packet racing, ACK: the format carries seq and the session excerpt, but none of the machinery, exactly like packet-up carries seq today without using it
- nothing about #4846's larger downlink freeze problem (the 15-20 KB per TCP connection cut): this only discards the CDN idle timer, it does not split data across connections

## Tests

- packet_down_test.go: frame round trip (with/without excerpt, with/without seq), byte-stream shaped like a socket, splitting payloads larger than one frame, padding skipped, malformed frame rejected, keep-alive written when idle, keep-alive suppressed while active, config normalization
- splithttp_test.go: full listen/dial round trip with packet-down on both end (100 KiB), and the fallback case with the client setting present but the server without one
- infra/conf: JSON un

issues.title: Outbound: Close the handler when removing it; VLESS Reverse Proxy: Don't start after closing
issues.body:
`outbound.Manager.RemoveHandler`, which `xray api rmo` (`HandlerService.RemoveOutbound`) calls, deletes the handler from the map but never closes it, while `inbound.Manager.RemoveHandler` does. So whatever the removed outbound's `Close()` would release keeps running:

- WireGuard creates its TUN in the constructor (a kernel TUN when available, otherwise a gVisor stack), and once used also has the device with its UDP socket and keepalives.
- VLESS with `reverse` keeps its monitor task: the removed outbound keeps dialing the server every 2 s.
- Same for MASQUE's tunnel. VLESS with `testpre` gets closed too, but its pre-connects only stop reliably with #7113: on main, `Close()` stops just the goroutines waiting to hand over a connection, not the ones redialing an unreachable server.

This shows up wherever outbounds are added and removed at runtime through the API, e.g. by panels.

### Changes

- `RemoveHandler` closes the handler it removed. It does so after releasing the manager lock, so a slow `Close()` (WireGuard) doesn't hold up `Select()`/`GetHandler()` for new connections. Removing an unknown tag still returns nil, and a removed handler is closed only once, since `Manager.Close()` no longer sees it.
- VLESS starts the reverse 2 s after the outbound is created (a goroutine in `New()`), so an outbound removed within those 2 s would still start it after `Close()`. `Reverse.Start()` is now a no-op once `Reverse.Close()` has run.

The other callers of `RemoveHandler` (commander, metrics, reverse portal, VLESS inbound's reverse) remove their own internal outbounds, whose `Close()` is a no-op or idempotent.

Connections already in flight on a removed outbound behave as before unless its `Close()` tears them down (WireGuard, MASQUE). A reverse bridge that is already connected is left to end on its own; only new ones stop.

### Reproduction (on 836a6fe)

Client: `api` with `HandlerService` behind a dokodemo-door inbound, `freedom` as the only configured outbound. Server: a plain TCP listener that only counts accepted connections.

**VLESS `reverse`**: the outbound is added with `xray api ado` and removed with `xray api rmo`. Afterwards `xray api lso` lists only the `freedom` outbound in all runs.

| `rmo` after `ado` | build | accepts at `rmo` | 3 s later | 13 s later |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 7 s | main | 3 | 4 | 9 |
| 7 s | this PR | 3 | 3 | 3 |
| 0.5 s | main | 0 | 1 | 6 |
| 0.5 s | this PR | 0 | 0 | 0 |

**WireGuard** (`noKernelTun: true`): five outbounds, each added with `ado` and removed right away with `rmo`. Goroutines from the `metrics` listener's `/debug/pprof/goroutine`: main 11 → 72, this PR 11 → 12.

### Tests

- New `TestRemoveHandlerClosesHandler` (on main the handler is closed 0 times) and `TestReverseNotStartedAfterClose` (on main the monitor runs once).
- `go test ./...` except `testing/scenarios`: the only failures also fail on main, tests that need `resources/geo*.dat` or network access.
- `go test ./testing/scenarios`: pass.
- `go run ./infra/vformat/main.go -mode check -pwd ./`: pass.

issues.title: Bound shutdown after termination signal
issues.body:
This change prevents Xray from waiting indefinitely during graceful shutdown after receiving SIGTERM or interrupt.

Previously, shutdown depended on the deferred server.Close() call returning. If any feature Close() path blocked, the process could stay alive while listeners or active connections continued operating. This made stale Xray processes difficult to detect, especially when another process could bind the same port.

Now Xray runs server.Close() explicitly after receiving a termination signal and waits up to 10 seconds. If shutdown does not complete in time, the process exits with code 1 so supervisors can treat it as a failed shutdown and avoid leaving a functional stale process behind.

This issue was most visible on mobile clients. Some apps, such as Telegram proxy-style traffic, may continue using an already-established path even when the VPN/client UI appears disabled. If the old Xray process remains alive during a stuck shutdown, those connections can continue transferring traffic and updating usage counters, making the node look stopped from the client side while traffic is still flowing server-side.

issues.title: TLS : tls spoofing
issues.body:
fix #5964

### RawPacket aka TLS Spoofing

So first lets talk about the idea,

when you connect to a xray server, the censors can see your TLS ClientHello, read the SNI, and figure out what you are doing and block :)

The RawPacket aka TLS spoofing fixes that by injecting a fake TLS ClientHello before the real one Hits.


The fake one carries like a decoy domain (ex. baidu.com) and then the real one carries your actual destination (ex. www.example.com).

A sensor that captures the first packet sees baidu.com and think that you are just browsing, and everything is okay with that, but in reality your connection goes through :)


It can be configured in the `finalmask.tcp` okay? and its only for client side.


### How everything works


When Xray dials a TCP connection and the first `Write()` happens (which also triggers the real TLS handshake) , our Raw Packet setup does the following.

1.builds a fake Tls ClientHello with whatever SNI you want or you have option to provide the raw bytes (b64).

2.Then we. wrap it in a raw TCP/ip packet.

3.Then deliberately we corrupt the TCP header using whatever method is selected okay?

4. Then we shoot it out via a raw socket

5. Then immediately let the real `Write()` go through normally


In short : two packets arrive at the server back to back and the fake one gets dropped by the servers TCP stack because of the corruption and then the real handshake proceeds like nothing happened.


### Config Example

```json
{
  "streamSettings": {
    "finalmask": {
      "tcp": [
        {
          "type": "rawpacket",
          "settings": {
            "sni": "baidu.com",
            "payload": "",
            "method": "wrong-sequence",
            "ttl": 3,
            "count": 1
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```


### Available Fields

`sni` : The domain to put in the fake ClientHello. If you set this, it will auto generate a valid TLS ClientHello for you automatically. If you set `payload` and `sni` same time , sni wins here.

```
"sni": "baidu.com"
```

`payload` : If you don't want an auto gnrated ClientHello, then just encode your raw bytes that you want into base64 and put them here. I have added an option to do it from command line also. Do like this 

```
 xray tls fake-hello google.com
 ```

It will out the thing and then just copy paste.


Note : If `sni` and payload are empty or not set , the raw packet does nothing and the connection goes through normally.


`method` : It defines how we corrupt the fake packet so the server drops it.

`wrong-sequence` : It duplicates the sequence number (looks like a retransmission so server drops it)

So we grab the kernels `snd_nxt` ( the next sequence number the kernel expects to send), then subtract the length of the fake payload and then use that as the sequence number of the injected packet. The results then is a duplicate of the. last segment, so the receivers TCP stack sees it as a retransmit at best, or like out of window at worst and then drops it.


`wrong-checksum`: It flips all the bits in the TCP checksum (so server sees a bad checksum and drops it)

We build the packet with a correct checksum and then flip every bit(^0xFFFF). The receiver then validates the checksum and its wrong, so the packet goes in trash.

`wrong-ack`: It sets ACK number way outside the receive window (so server sends dup ACK then drops it)

It sets the ACK number to `rcv_nxt - window/2` and that's way outside of the receivers window, and the kernel responds with a dup ACK containing the correct sequence number, then drops it.

`wrong-md5` : This adds a fake TCP MD5 signature option and server without MD5 drops it

Here we append a TCP option with kind=19 and length=18 to the TCP header. The kind 19 is the MD5 signature option (RFC 2385), if the receiver doesn't use TCP MD5 (which is basically everything except some BGP routers), it sees an unknown option

issues.body:
This PR moves Browser Dialer usage to `sockopt.dialerProxy` with `browser://host:port/uuid` URLs and removes the earlier parse-time listener startup side effects.

### What changed

- `dialerProxy` now uses `browser://host:port/uuid`
- Browser Dialer URLs are collected and validated during config build
- URL validation includes host:port parsing, UUID path validation, and same-port/different-IP conflict checks
- Browser Dialer remains restricted to WebSocket and XHTTP, with XHTTP limited to `auto` / `packet-up`, and REALITY rejected
- Listener startup is now controlled by the Xray instance lifecycle:
